cards.title: The after-flash pattern is reassurance, not an alarm
cards.applies-when: A Drive starts with a Fuel-quality score above the Baseline after a Flash.
cards.body: After every new Flash KTuner sets the Fuel-quality score to 0.59, and it falls back to the Baseline with calm driving. A start at or below 0.60 that settles toward 0.49 is what a fresh flash does. It is never an Unexplained change, and it never sets a Verdict on its own. Give it ten to fifteen calm minutes before judging fuel or heat, because the score needs that long to relearn. If the score does not settle, or if it climbs again in traffic, that later rise is the finding, judged on its own. The Shakedown drive exists for exactly this pattern.

cards.title: Boost By Gear Limits only limit, and yours are off
cards.applies-when: The owner asks about Boost By Gear, or how KTuner protects a CVT.
cards.body: Boost By Gear Limits is one table per gear, rpm by atmospheric pressure, and it only limits: wherever the boost table asks less, the table wins, so values above every target mean no limit. Your map holds 35.4 psi everywhere, so no gear limit is active. KTuner's own tool for sparing a CVT is a first-gear limit, and its quick settings offer flat or ramped versions. The app explains it and does not write this table, and which gear number your CVT reports to it is unconfirmed.

cards.title: Boost codes P0046 and P0299, and what to log
cards.applies-when: The owner reports P0046 or P0299, a limp with a dead pedal, or boost that misses target.
cards.body: P0046 means the ECU can't hold the wastegate where it commands it. On this generation owners traced it to a sticking wastegate actuator, and to a pinhole leak in the vacuum line on the charge pipe; a new downpipe seemed to fix it only for a while. P0299 is underboost. In your log, compare EWG Position with EWG Target, and boost with its target: a position that doesn't follow its target points to the actuator; boost under target with the wastegate shut points to a leak or the turbo's limit. Fix the hardware first; no map change.

cards.title: More boost, one proven step at a time
cards.applies-when: The owner asks for more boost, or asks how a boost raise would be proven.
cards.body: A Boost step adds 1 psi to Boost Target 2 Normal, Low and High cam, 3,500 to 4,500 rpm rows, never above the Final Boost Target peak, 23.4 here. Only the second tune gets it; a proven step is copied to the others. Offered when the latest Cool drive holds two floored pulls held 4 seconds above 3,500 rpm and a hot drive passes too. Floored is pedal 85 percent or more until a key-on reading sets it: on these cars floored reads 100 to 113, yours never above 94. Gates: target moved; under- and overshoot held half a second within 1.5 psi, total at most 24; timing within 1 degree of the last proven version; Knock Control settled, at most 0.56 below 5,200 rpm; mixture never leaner than 12.0; fuel pressure at least 90 percent of target. The first failure undoes it.

cards.title: CVT care is heat management, not a torque number
cards.applies-when: Any reply that judges CVT fluid temperature, slip, or hard driving in heat.
cards.body: The old keep-torque-under-a-number warning is removed: the app sets no torque number for this car, but the ECU's own factory torque limiter still protects the CVT and can pull boost back. What the logs can judge is fluid heat and slip. Watch starts at 90 °C of fluid temperature, and Stop at 100 °C is provisional, not yet seen on this car, whose peak is 95 °C. No pulls with the fluid at or above 90 °C, and never brake-launch: failures owners report come from launching and heavy low-end torque, not from steady pulls. Slip shows as revs jumping without speed, with zero such events across all drives here. The fluid is the Honda HCF-2 grade, changed on the severe schedule on a tuned car in hot traffic.

cards.title: Catted or catless downpipe: which one, and what each costs
cards.applies-when: The owner asks which downpipe to buy, or whether a catless pipe is worth it.
cards.body: The 400-cell catted pipes from TSP and RV6 claim no warning light, and most owners report none, though a few see the rear-sensor code P2A01, or a light only in heavy rain or on long highway runs: that is still the shop's pick. The 200-cell 27WON pipe sets P0420 for most owners within days. Catless makes about 0 to 6 whp over a good catted pipe (owner and vendor reports), brings exhaust smell into the cabin, always sets P0420, and risks the đăng kiểm tailpipe gas test; an unapproved modification can also be fined 65 to 75 million VND. The tune response is the same for all three: no map change, and a small boost trim only if a log proves boost holds above target. Ask which pipe is fitted: older RV6 pipes were 300-cell.

cards.title: What a downpipe changes on this car, and what it doesn't
cards.applies-when: The owner has fitted or plans a downpipe, or asks what the map should change for it.
cards.body: A downpipe lowers the back pressure after the turbo, so the same boost arrives a little sooner; on Civic X dynos torque came 200 to 400 rpm earlier. The parts vendor claims +7 to +12 whp with no tune; no independent dyno exists for this car. Your logs were all recorded with the downpipe and front pipe fitted, so that gain is already in them. No Honda tuner changes the map for a downpipe on the stock turbo, and nothing changes on fuel or spark: the full-load target stays 11.0 and timing is untouched. The one possible map action is a small boost trim, and only if a log proves boost holds above target. After fitting, check both flanges for leaks with the engine cold: a leak shows on the rear oxygen sensor and the catalyst code, not on the front A/F sensor.

cards.title: The Baseline drive brief, step by step
cards.applies-when: Before the first log, after a Flash or Install, or whenever the owner asks how to log a drive the app can read.
cards.body: Log it like a shop asks. Before you drive: in TunerView turn on every gauge the app reads (AFR Command and MAF Hz included) and set the fastest rate it offers, 10 Hz or more. Go before 8 am or after an hour parked in shade, so the intake is under 42 °C. Drive 10 minutes normally until coolant is above 80 °C. Cruise steady at several speeds for trims. Then, on a straight, empty, legal road, in S: from a 50 km/h roll press the pedal fully and hold it to 100 km/h, then lift. Cruise a minute to cool and do the second pull, starting with intake under 48 °C. Keep at least 10 minutes of moving time in the log, then export the CSV.

cards.title: How KTuner picks between the dual boost targets
cards.applies-when: The owner asks what the ECO button does to boost, or which boost table is in use.
cards.body: Dual Boost Targets With ECO Button gives each tune two boost tables: on the 1.5T the ECU uses Boost Target ECO while the ECO button is on and Boost Target Normal otherwise, so Sport runs the Normal table too. On Starter 21 Dual Tune 2 that is 18 psi in ECO and 21 psi in Normal. The button is the switch: no flash, no device. Use ECO on hot days, in traffic, or on fuel you don't trust. No log channel records ECO, so note it when you attach a log and compare only drives in the same mode.

cards.title: E10 needs no extra fuel and no trim offset
cards.applies-when: The owner asks about E10, fuel quality, or adding fuel for ethanol.
cards.body: Pure gasoline burns at 14.7 and ethanol at 9.0, so E10 lands at 14.1 and needs about 4.3 percent more fuel by mass for the same lambda. The ECU delivers that itself: the front sensor and the trims in closed loop, the fuel model in open loop. E10 carries about 3.4 percent less energy per litre, so economy drops a little and nothing else changes. Vietnam RON95 is about US 90 by Honda's own octane scale and 90 to 91 by the usual estimate: at or just under the 91 that KTuner asks for. Cruise trims sit near 0.8 percent negative on E10, so no E10 offset is ever written into the airflow curve, and WOT stays judged against the map's own target.

cards.title: The turbo has no headroom left on this map
cards.applies-when: The owner asks for more boost or more power, or a reply explains a flat pull.
cards.body: The Starter 21 map asks 18 psi in ECO and 21 psi in Normal and Sport, and the file tops out at 23.4 psi of final target. These logs were measured with a downpipe and front pipe already fitted: at the highest boost logged, up to 19.9 psi, the wastegate sits about 2.5 percent open, against 8.0 percent at idle and cruise and 65.5 percent at its most open. Nearly all exhaust already drives the turbine, so more boost mostly means more heat, not more power. KTuner claims the map adds up to 58 lb-ft, or 79 Nm, over a stock car rated 240 Nm and 176 hp. Gains from here come from cooler air and good habits, and more boost only from a step proven on your logs. Most drives end with no map change, and that is an answer, not a gap.

cards.title: Final Boost Target passes the target through and caps it
cards.applies-when: The owner asks what Final Boost Target does, or whether it limits boost.
cards.body: Final Boost Target takes the incoming target, from the boost table, the part-pedal target or the Boost By Gear limit, passes it nearly one to one, and caps it at its last column header. Raising that cap means changing the header and its whole column. On your map every column is the same in every rpm row and the top is 23.4 psi, so it passes your target through and is not what holds a pull below the table. The app explains it and never edits it.

cards.title: Flashing with KTuner: power, the key, and what is normal after
cards.applies-when: The owner is about to flash, a flash failed, or warning lights came on after a flash.
cards.body: Put a battery charger on the car and power the V2 from a strong port: low voltage is what fails flashes. Ignition on, engine off, never running. When it finishes, key off for ten seconds, back on, and wait for flash successful. Warning lights during the flash are normal, and driver-assist warnings can stay until you have driven ten to fifteen minutes. A failed flash leaves the car unable to start: reconnect and accept recovery, which returns it to factory. A Recovery prompt while the engine runs means a loose cable: say no. Error codes right after a flash usually mean the wrong codebase: start the tune with the one that matches the unit info. If the V2 stops waking with the car, set CAN Gateway to Yes. Saving a tune to the V2 is not flashing it: the next log proves the change.

cards.title: Is premium fuel worth it? Test it tank against tank
cards.applies-when: The owner asks whether E10 RON97 III is worth it, or logs a drive on a different fuel.
cards.body: Better fuel is judged by Knock Control, tank against tank, never by feel. Petrolimex sells no RON97; smaller retailers sell E10 RON97 III. On cool drives both fuels sit at the 0.49 floor, so only a hot pair can show a difference. Drive your usual E10 RON95 III until Knock Control settles, then log a hot drive. Run the tank low, fill E10 RON97 III, drive calmly until it settles again, and log the same hot drive: same route, same mode, same map slot, intake within 8 °C. Tag each log with its fuel. Read Knock Control and timing at or below 5,200 rpm only, because above that the ECU raises the score on purpose. A gap of 0.5 degrees or less is inside KTuner's logging step: no measurable gain. The most RON97 can win back is what heat costs, about 1.6 degrees.

cards.title: Heat soak, not the tune, costs this car performance
cards.applies-when: A Drive runs hot, pulls start with hot intake air, or boost falls on a hot afternoon.
cards.body: Every drive started soon after another one begins with 57 to 64 °C in the manifold. Cool drives read 35 to 39 °C while moving, and a pull should start at or below 48 °C. The intercooler is not the problem: under boost it adds only 2 to 6 °C over the inlet air. Two drives half an hour apart prove it: pull-start intake 49 °C against 60 °C, peak boost 19.9 psi against 16.7 psi, and the timed run 1.77 s against 2.23 s. After a hot stop, drive three to five calm minutes before any hard acceleration, and judge power only between drives at similar intake temperatures.

cards.title: Score rises above 5,200 rpm do not count while the artificial rise is on
cards.applies-when: A Drive shows Fuel-quality score rises at high revs.
cards.body: Non-Si ECUs raise Knock Control on purpose above about 5,200 rpm. KTuner can remove it with Quick Enables, Eliminate Artificial Knock Control Rise; on this car's Starter map that box is off, so the rise is present, and the Car profile records the box. While it is off, those rises say nothing about fuel quality or heat and are excluded from fuel and heat verdicts; the forced rise costs about 2 degrees only at the top of a pull. If the box is ever ticked, a rise up there is real knock and counts like any other. This owner rarely revs past 5,200 rpm. Judge the tank by what the score does in normal driving and in traffic, where heat and lugging are the real movers.

cards.title: Why hot intake air costs power: IAT Ignition
cards.applies-when: The owner asks why the car feels slower when hot, or what intake temperature does to timing.
cards.body: Hot intake air costs timing on a schedule, before any knock. This map's IAT Ignition High Load (Retard) takes nothing up to 40 °C, 4.5 degrees at 50 °C and 9 degrees at 90 °C and above; at low load it takes 1 to 3 degrees. KTuner applies it through the knock limit, so it can take up to that much as the air heats, and on E10 RON95 Knock Control rises in heat and pulls more on top. That is why a heat-soaked pull makes less power on the same map, and why the cure is cooler intake air and a few calm minutes after a hot stop, not a map change.

cards.title: IAT is after the intercooler, IAT2 before the turbo
cards.applies-when: The owner asks what IAT2 measures, or a reply would judge the intercooler from IAT2.
cards.body: On this car IAT is the manifold air after the intercooler and IAT2 the inlet air before the turbo. Under boost IAT reads 2 to 6 °C above IAT2, which only works that way round, and KTuner's gauge names and owners of the same engine label them the same. So the intercooler is judged by IAT minus IAT2 under boost: a gap that grows over back-to-back pulls means it is saturating. Some owners report other ECUs of this engine the other way round, so on a new car check the sign of the gap before trusting it.

cards.title: How the ECU sets final ignition, with KTuner's own example
cards.applies-when: The owner asks how timing is decided, why Actual Ign is lower than the table, or what Knock Retard means.
cards.body: KTuner's help gives the rule: ignition table plus knock ignition limitation, minus knock retard, is the final timing, and the ECU uses the lesser of that and the table, so it never runs more than the table. Knock retard is Knock Control times the knock retard table. Their example: 21 plus 2 is 23 degrees; Knock Control 0.38 times a table value of 10 is 3.8 degrees of retard, so the final is 19.2. The log shows both in steps and cuts down rather than rounding: the example logs the retard as 3.5. On TunerView, ignition and retard both move in half-degree steps; the one-degree ignition step is for OBD loggers. Under boost every score from 0.49 to 0.54 logs the same 5 degrees of retard, so read Knock Control itself. Follow Actual Ign, Knock Control and Knock Retard together, and never read meaning into a half-degree change.

cards.title: The gauges the shop reads, by their KTuner names
cards.applies-when: The owner asks which gauges to log, what a gauge abbreviation means, or why a log reads Can't tell.
cards.body: KTuner's short gauge names and the CSV's long names are the same gauges. K.Cont is Knock Control, the Fuel-quality score; K.Ret is Knock Retard; A.Ignition is Ignition. TC.Target and TC.Press are Turbo Pressure Target and Turbo Pressure, read at the turbo before the throttle, while MAP is the manifold. EWG.Posi and EWG.Target are the wastegate; DIFPress and DIFP.Target are fuel pressure; Wideband is the O2 column. TPS is your foot on the pedal and TPS.C is TPS Command, the throttle plate. Log bank one trims only: a trim pinned at its lowest value is a wrong bank or a dead channel and reads Can't tell. Your logger already records all of these; still missing are AFR Command and MAF Hz, which the airflow and mixture checks need. Knock Count is a misfire count, not knock.

cards.title: Is the log good enough to read?
cards.applies-when: Every upload, before any verdict; when a log settles nothing.
cards.body: A tuner checks the log before the car. Four things make a log readable: a fast enough rate (10 samples a second or more), at least 10 minutes of moving time, no gauge stuck on one number while the revs move, and AFR Command and MAF Hz in the gauge list. Without AFR Command the mixture can only be judged against the map's target, not what the ECU actually asked for; without MAF Hz the airflow sensor's headroom can't be checked. A log that misses the gate is not a failure of the car: fix the logger and drive the brief again.

cards.title: What a log needs before the airflow curve can be corrected
cards.applies-when: Before any MAF Scaling change, or the owner asks how much driving a MAF correction needs.
cards.body: A MAF correction is only as good as the samples behind each point. The method MAF tools use: an engine fully warm, intake temperature steady, throttle smooth, and the rows around sudden throttle changes, stops and loop transitions thrown away. Each point is corrected from the trims logged at that airflow, averaged so one odd moment can't move it, and a point with too few samples is left alone. The usual guide is at least 30 min of steady cruising, as much mixed driving, and 15 min of slow driving across rounds. Smooth the result once, lightly. Fix part throttle first, then full throttle. Expect two or three rounds: nobody nails it in one shot.

cards.title: MAF Scaling follows the housing, never the brand
cards.applies-when: An intake is fitted, trims sit far off after a Flash, or the owner asks which MAF preset to pick.
cards.body: Ask which housing is fitted before touching anything: factory airbox, a street housing, or a larger Race housing. The street housings read near stock, so they keep the Factory curve. The Race curves read 1.29 to 1.43 times the air at the same sensor frequency, so a Race preset on a street housing runs about forty percent rich and the trims clamp trying to pull it back. After any airflow Flash, drive calm first and make no pull until trims sit within 5 percent. Trims beyond 10 percent across most of the range mean the curve is wrong for the hardware: revert, do not tune around it. Never infer the housing from the brand.

cards.title: Which way a trim moves the airflow curve
cards.applies-when: The owner asks how to correct MAF Scaling from a CSV, or which way a trim points.
cards.body: A positive trim means the ECU added fuel because it measured too little air, so the airflow points covering that airflow move up by about that percent; a negative trim moves them down. Average the trims at each point over warm, steady driving, and throw away the rows where you lift off or coast, which read zero or spike, and the first seconds after a throttle change. Reach the higher points with a slow, steady roll-on, not a stab. Apply part of the correction, keep the curve rising, flash, and log again. On this car only rows below about 8 psi count: above that the trims freeze. Owners and KTuner staff describe the same method.

cards.title: How tuners correct the full-throttle end of the airflow curve
cards.applies-when: The owner asks how to correct MAF from a CSV, or full-throttle mixture is far from AFR Command.
cards.body: At full throttle the airflow table is corrected against AFR Command, not against trims. Log several full-throttle pulls in the same gear mode at the same intake temperature, with AFR Command and MAF Hz logged. Where the measured mixture is leaner than commanded, the points covering that airflow read too little air; where it is richer, too much. Change only those points, by about 2 % per round, keep the curve smooth, flash, and log the same pulls again. Stop when the mixture sits a little richer than commanded, about 0.2 AFR. Richer than 10.5 means the points are too high. One owner's numbers are never copied to another car, and a blind fixed cut to the top of the curve is not a calibration. Done wrong, this leans the engine at full load, so the shop checks every point before you flash.

cards.title: How KTuner on-the-fly map switching works
cards.applies-when: The owner asks about map slots, Tune 1, 2 or 3, or switching maps while driving.
cards.body: On The Fly Map Switching holds three tunes in one map. They differ only in boost targets and Turbo Responsiveness; ignition, fuel, knock and the throttle setting are shared by all three, so a tune cannot carry a fuel's timing. Switch with a long press of the cruise Cancel button; switching while moving is supported. With the KTuner device unplugged the car starts in Tune 1, so Tune 1 holds the proven map and a trial goes in Tune 2. As digitized, the three tunes on this map hold the same boost targets, so switching changes nothing yet. No log channel records the tune: tag each log with its map slot and switch only between logs.

cards.title: The Misfire and count gauges are not the ones to judge by
cards.applies-when: The owner worries about a Knock Count or Misfire number in TunerView, or asks which gauge matters.
cards.body: On the 1.5T, the Knock Count and Misfire gauges are not the ones to judge by. KTuner support told owners that the count is tied to misfire detection, and experienced owners ignore both on this platform. The number that matters is the Fuel-quality score: it is the ECU's learned margin, and it is what the shop reads. AFR Adj is not the mixture to watch either: watch the measured AFR against AFR Command. So a rising count on its own is no reason to buy spark plugs or change the map; a step up in the Fuel-quality score is.

cards.title: Don't add octane booster
cards.applies-when: The owner asks about octane booster or additives.
cards.body: Don't add octane booster. KTuner staff, a vendor and the long-running owner reliability thread all advise against it, and one engine failure in the largest owner census lists booster as a possible cause. If you suspect the fuel, try a different busy station, or E10 RON97, and compare tank against tank by Knock Control on matched drives.

cards.title: Oil grade and keeping the revs up
cards.applies-when: A Drive shows lugging, or the owner asks about oil for a tuned car.
cards.body: Use the Honda manual grade 0W-20, rated API SP or newer: those ratings pass an engine test that averages five or fewer early-ignition events per run and never more than eight, while plain older grades require no such test. Lugging means 900 to 1,700 rpm with the foot down, and 31 of all 41 score rises on this car happened there, so the case against it is data, not theory. Below 60 km/h in traffic, use S or a paddle before pressing past a third of the pedal, and let it rev to 2000 rpm or more first. Its top end touches the 1,500 to 2,500 rpm low-speed early-ignition band, which is a second reason to stay out of it.

cards.title: Under boost the trims stop correcting the mixture
cards.applies-when: The owner asks why trims look fine but full-throttle mixture is off, or what open loop means.
cards.body: On this car it is confirmed from the logs: short-term trim reads exactly zero on every warm row at 12 psi and above, and on nearly all from about 8 psi, while lower down it moves as normal. So under boost the ECU runs open loop: the trims neither correct the mixture nor say anything about the airflow curve there, and only the airflow calibration (MAF Scaling) and the map's target decide it. An airflow correction uses only rows below about 8 psi, where the trims are live. Judge full-throttle mixture against AFR Command, the value the ECU actually asked for, which can differ from the table. Read the loop state from the trims, never from a status number alone.

cards.title: P0420 after a downpipe, and the inspection risk
cards.applies-when: A downpipe is fitted, P0420 appears, or the owner asks about switching the code off.
cards.body: A downpipe carries the rear oxygen sensor, the one the catalyst check reads; the front A/F sensor threads into the turbo outlet and does not move. So a downpipe flange leak shows on the rear sensor and the catalyst code, not on fuel trims. Most 200-cell pipes set P0420 within days; owners of 400-cell pipes report none. An oxygen sensor spacer is hit-and-miss: it can swap P0420 for a slow-response P1039. In KTuner the switch lives under Main Parameters, then Disables and Monitors, at the P0420 catalyst efficiency entry, and this car keeps it on. The đăng kiểm inspection tests tailpipe gas and checks that the warning lamp works; switching the code off hides a fault and does nothing for the gas test. Prefer a 400-cell catted pipe, check both flanges for leaks with the engine cold, and keep the monitor on.

cards.title: More air, more fire, more fuel? Where power comes from
cards.applies-when: The owner asks how to make more power or torque, or asks for more fuel, more timing or more boost.
cards.body: Only air makes power. Torque follows the mass of air trapped in each cylinder, and boost is a pressure, not a flow. Fuel follows air: best power sits near lambda 0.82 to 0.85, and this map asks 0.75 on purpose to cool the charge against knock and keep turbine heat down, so more fuel adds nothing and leaner is wrong on hot E10 RON95. Spark is capped by knock before its best point on pump fuel, so more boost on this fuel forces timing out: about the same power, more heat. Honda's ECU is torque-based: the pedal asks for torque, the ECU sets boost and throttle, and its factory torque limiter caps the result to protect the CVT. A downpipe makes the same air cheaper to get; it does not lift that cap.

cards.title: Throttle response and turbo lag live in Quick Adjustments
cards.applies-when: The owner asks for sharper throttle response, less turbo lag, or about Early Spool.
cards.body: Response and lag live in KTuner's Quick Adjustments dropdowns, not in map tables, and on this car every level is Factory: Throttle Responsiveness, Boost Target Ramp Rate and each tune's Turbo Responsiveness. Throttle Responsiveness is pedal feel, not power, and no log can prove it, so it is your taste. For lag, a floored pull shows the cause: time from the pedal at 85 percent to boost at 90 percent of target, read with the wastegate. If the target ramps slowly while the wastegate is still open, one level up on Turbo Responsiveness or Boost Target Ramp Rate can help, one change at a time, proven on matched pulls. If the wastegate is shut and boost still lags, that is the turbo itself and no setting helps. Early Spool stays off: it adds low-rpm torque where the CVT and pre-ignition risk sit. The app explains these; it never writes them.

cards.title: Knock Control ranges and what each level costs
cards.applies-when: Any reply that names a Knock Control level or a timing cost.
cards.body: The Fuel-quality score reads 0.49 at its best, and higher means timing is pulled everywhere. Watch starts at 0.56. No hard driving starts at 0.62 held over 60 seconds. Stop starts at 0.80, which this car has never reached. Under boost each point above the floor costs 10.2 degrees, so 0.56 costs about 0.7 degrees, 0.62 costs about 1.3 degrees, 0.65 costs about 1.6 degrees, and 0.80 would cost about 3.2 degrees. The 5.0 degrees of retard logged under boost at 0.49 is scheduled from the score, not knock events. Cool drives end at 0.49 to 0.53, and the hottest traffic drive stayed below the 0.66 maximum seen on this car. The cut points are judgement, labelled as such, not measured limits.

cards.title: My full-throttle mixture reads richer than the map asks
cards.applies-when: The owner asks whether a rich full-throttle reading is a fault, or blames E10.
cards.body: The map asks 11.0 at full load, which is 0.75 in lambda, and this car reads 10.1 to 10.7 there, or 0.69 to 0.73 against the 0.75 asked. Richer than asked is the safe side for knock and heat, not a fault, though it costs a little power: best power sits leaner, near 0.82 to 0.85. Every logged reading sits at 11.3 or richer. E10 does not make it lean: the sensor measures lambda whatever the fuel, and no fuel is added for E10. The mixture is judged at 12 psi and above, where the full-load target applies. Watch starts half an AFR leaner than asked, and danger starts at 12.0, a full AFR leaner. Without the live lambda command channel, lower-load cells with leaner targets stay out of the verdict.

cards.title: The Shakedown drive after any Flash
cards.applies-when: A Flash was just recorded, or the Next step asks for a calm proving drive.
cards.body: After any Flash, drive calm for 10 minutes before any hard acceleration: steady speeds, no pulls, engine fully warm. Watch the trims first and the score second. Hard driving waits until a calm stretch shows trims within 5 percent; that is what proves the new map measures air correctly. Save the earlier file under its own name before flashing, so Undo is one flash back. If the trims never settle, or a new Stop appears on the Shakedown itself, flash back and say so: the Flash is not credited until a drive proves it.

cards.title: The boost tables in KTuner
cards.applies-when: The owner asks what a boost table does, wants more boost, or a boost change is in the plan.
cards.body: Each of the three tunes has its own Boost Target tables, Normal and ECO, each Low and High cam: rpm by load tables of the boost the ECU aims for. On this map Normal plateaus at 21 psi from 4,000 rpm, ECO keeps factory-like boost, and as digitized the three tunes hold the same values. Final Boost Target is the target after the ECU arbitrates, topping out near 23.4. Boost By Gear Limits is flat, so no gear limit is active. The logged target has never passed 19.2 psi: the factory throttle dampening and the Boost Target Ramp Rate hold it, so it follows the pedal and climbs over seconds. Cylinder Fill Limitation is a knock safeguard; the everyday cap is the factory torque limiter, which KTuner does not expose. Low-rpm torque is what hurts the CVT, so good maps keep boost down there. Change the paired tables together.

cards.title: Ignition tables: read them, don't add timing on the street
cards.applies-when: The owner asks about ignition, timing or knock-sensitivity tables, or asks for more timing.
cards.body: Ignition Base (Low and High cam) is the main spark map by rpm and load; Ignition Max is a ceiling; Ethanol Ign Adj adds timing for ethanol; the Knock Sens tables set how sensitive knock detection is. KTuner's own formula: final timing is the ignition table plus the knock limit, minus the timing Knock Control pulls. Best timing can't be seen from a street log, so the street rule is: start from a professional basemap, log Knock Control trends over several pulls, and only ever remove timing, in steps of 1 to 2 degrees, where retard collects. Never add timing or lower knock sensitivity without a dyno. This app reads these tables but doesn't edit them.

cards.title: The airflow (MAF Scaling) table comes first
cards.applies-when: Trims are off, an intake was fitted, or the owner asks what MAF Scaling does.
cards.body: MAF Scaling turns the airflow sensor's frequency into grams of air, over 103 points. Every fuel calculation starts from it, which is why tuners fix airflow before anything else. Presets exist per intake housing: Factory, and Race presets for the larger housings; Custom is the one you edit. A tuner corrects it from steady part-throttle trims, bin by bin, applying only part of the correction each round and keeping the curve smooth, then flashes and logs again until trims sit within about 5 percent. Up to about 10 percent is commonly called normal; beyond that the table, or the preset, is wrong.

cards.title: WOT Enrichment is the full-throttle mixture target
cards.applies-when: The owner asks about AFR, lambda or WOT Enrichment, or a mixture change is in the plan.
cards.body: WOT Enrichment (WOT Enrich in the map file; its load axis is the air per stroke, in milligrams) holds the mixture the ECU aims for, by rpm and load, Low and High cam. KTuner's Nominal Lambda for Component Protection page is for the Type R, not this car. Cruise and light load stay at 14.7 for the catalyst; the highest load columns ask 11.0. It is a target, not a fix: change it only after the airflow table is right, with trims within 5 percent, and in steps of 0.2 AFR or less, watching Knock Control on every pull. Leaner at full throttle trades knock and exhaust heat margin for a little power; richer than asked is safe. Low and High are changed together.

cards.title: Should I add 2 or 5 percent timing?
cards.applies-when: The owner asks to add timing by a percentage, or to try more timing and see what happens.
cards.body: No. Honda's ECU never runs more timing than Ignition Base; it only takes timing away through Knock Control, and on E10 RON95 this car already sits at the 0.49 floor under boost, so the table is the timing. A percent works the wrong way here: Ignition Base holds 150 negative cells, the high-load ones where boost lives, and plus 5 percent makes them more negative, about 0.08 degrees less on a typical boosted cell, while it adds about 1 degree in cruise cells that are already near ideal. Every tuner works in degrees and adds timing only on a dyno, keeping 2 to 3 degrees from knock. On the street the sound move is the reverse: remove timing in degrees where Knock Control rises repeatably. That stays teach-only here until a load channel is logged.

cards.title: The trim pattern names one cause
cards.applies-when: Trims are off and the owner changed something, or a Stop names trims.
cards.body: Trims beyond 10 percent in every load band, from the first minute, right after a Flash or a fitted part, usually mean the airflow preset does not match the intake housing. Trims 15 percent or worse everywhere after a change mean Undo first: flash back the earlier file, then pick the preset for the housing. Trims wrong only at idle and low airflow, fine higher up, usually mean unmetered air, a leak after the sensor: check clamps and flanges with the engine cold, no map change. Never bend the airflow curve to cancel a preset mismatch, and never touch full-throttle targets for a trim fault. Prove it with a calm drive and trims within 5 percent.

cards.title: Trims within 5 percent are fine, beyond 10 is a Stop
cards.applies-when: Any reply that judges fuel trims or air measurement.
cards.body: Trims within 5 percent either way are fine, and beyond 10 percent either way is a Stop. On this car warm cruise trims sit at a median of 0.8 percent negative, with the middle band from 3.1 percent negative to 1.6 percent positive, all on E10, so there is no E10 offset to subtract. The one fault drive sat at 28 percent negative median total trim, far outside anything healthy. A Stop here means the ECU cannot measure air correctly, so hard driving waits until a calm drive shows trims back within 5 percent. The cause comes from the trim pattern, never from the size of the number alone.

cards.title: How a careful tuner changes a map from logs
cards.applies-when: The owner asks how tuning from logs works, or wants to change several things at once.
cards.body: Read the whole log before touching anything, and remember which cells you already changed so no cell is corrected twice from the same evidence. Change one thing per round: fuel or airflow first, log again, and only then look at spark. Apply only part of what the log suggests, then let the next log show the rest. Judge with the engine fully warm, from mid-gear pulls, never first gear, and roll into the throttle instead of stabbing it. Never add timing on the street. After hard logging, let a turbo engine idle a minute before switching off. A Knock Count blip alone can be noise; repeated evidence decides.

cards.title: The order a tuner works in
cards.applies-when: Before any map change, and when the owner asks why one table comes before another.
cards.body: Every log is read in the same order. First, is the log usable. Second, safety: anything lean under boost, a step up in Knock Control, fuel pressure under target, or heat — stop and find the cause. Third, air before fuel: trims against airflow show whether the airflow table matches the intake; never fix a scaling error with fuel targets. Fourth, fuel against its target under boost. Spark is the ECU's job: rising Knock Control means less margin, and the remedy is fuel, heat or boost, not more timing on the street. Then boost, actual against target. One change, one reflash, one log under the same conditions.

cards.title: Leaning the full-throttle mixture can cost timing, not add power
cards.applies-when: The owner asks to lean the full-throttle target for power, or why the mixture lever is locked.
cards.body: An owner who calibrated his own 1.5T found that running full-throttle mixture near or past 11.5 made the ECU pull timing hard, so it lost power instead of gaining it; 11 to 11.2 worked best on his car. That is one car, not a rule, but it is the same direction this car's data points: no gain shown from leaning, and a real risk. That is why the shop keeps the full-throttle mixture target where the basemap has it. What would change that is a log with AFR Command, the car healthy in heat, and a like-for-like proof drive.
